The magnitude of the charge on an electron is the elementary charge,
\(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C,
as determined by Millikan's oil drop experiment (Sec. 10.3.2).

This is the smallest free charge observed in nature, and it is why charge is quantized: the charge on any object must be an integral multiple of it, \(q = \pm ne\), where \(n\) is an integer. An electron carries \(-e\) and a proton \(+e\), so the two are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, which is what makes ordinary matter electrically neutral.

Law of conservation of charge: for an isolated system the total charge can neither be created nor destroyed. In any given physical process charge may get transferred from one part of the system to another, but the total charge of the system remains constant (Sec. 10.3.3).

The chapter's illustration is the rubbing of a glass rod with silk. The rod becomes positively charged and the silk negatively charged, and the positive charge on the glass is found to be exactly equal to the negative charge on the silk. No charge has been created: electrons have simply been transferred from the glass to the silk. The glass-and-silk system therefore still possesses zero net charge after rubbing, exactly as it did before.

One coulomb is the amount of charge which, when placed at a distance of one metre from another charge of the same magnitude in vacuum, experiences a force of \(9.0 \times 10^{9}\) N (Sec. 10.4.3).

This definition comes straight from Coulomb's law. In free space
\(F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r^{2}} = 9 \times 10^{9}\dfrac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r^{2}}\)
Putting \(q_{1} = q_{2} = q\) and \(r = 1.0\) m gives \(F = 9 \times 10^{9}q^{2}\), which equals \(9.0 \times 10^{9}\) N precisely when \(q = 1\) C.

That force is enormous, so the coulomb is a very large unit of charge. In electrostatics the sub-units microcoulomb (\(10^{-6}\) C), nanocoulomb (\(10^{-9}\) C) and picocoulomb (\(10^{-12}\) C) are the ones normally used.

[Textbook misprint: the question asks for the "strength of electric charge" while supplying a potential difference and a plate separation, which between them determine the electric FIELD and not a charge. It is answered as the field, \(E = V/d\).]

Note first that the question asks for the strength of the electric charge, but a potential difference and a plate separation do not determine a charge; they determine the electric FIELD between the plates. That is the quantity the chapter's own Example 10.5 obtains from exactly this data, and it is what is found here.

Between a pair of parallel plates the field is uniform and is given by
\(E = \dfrac{V}{d}\)  (Sec. 10.6.2)
Given \(V = 10\) V and \(d = 0.5\) mm \(= 0.5 \times 10^{-3}\) m,
\(E = \dfrac{10}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 2 \times 10^{4}\) V/m

So the strength of the electric field between the plates is \(2 \times 10^{4}\) V/m, equivalently \(2 \times 10^{4}\) N/C, directed from the positive plate towards the negative plate.

A uniform electric field is one which has the same magnitude and the same direction at every point of the region being considered.

Its lines of force are therefore parallel to one another and equally spaced, which is characteristic (8) of the properties of lines of force listed in Sec. 10.6.3. The two halves of that description matter separately: parallel lines mean the direction does not change from point to point, and equal spacing means the magnitude does not change either, since the density of the lines measures the strength of the field.

The standard way of producing such a field is the pair of charged parallel plates of Sec. 10.6.2; in the region between the plates the field is uniform, with magnitude \(E = V/d\). By contrast the field of a point charge is radial and falls off as \(1/r^{2}\), so it is non-uniform in both direction and magnitude.

It would mean that the electric field has two different directions at that one point, which is impossible. This is why two lines of force can never intersect.

The reason lies in the definition of a line of force: it is a curve drawn so that the tangent at any point on it gives the direction of the electric field at that point (Sec. 10.6.3). If two lines crossed at a point, two different tangents could be drawn there, and so the field would have two directions at a single place. But the electric field at a point is the force experienced by a unit positive charge placed there, and a force has one definite magnitude and one definite direction. The field therefore cannot have two directions at once.

Characteristic (2) of the chapter's list states exactly this: the lines of force neither intersect nor meet each other, as it will mean that the electric field has two directions at a single point.

The SI unit of linear charge density is the coulomb per metre, C/m, that is C m\(^{-1}\) (Sec. 10.10).

Linear charge density \(\lambda\) is defined for a charge distributed uniformly along a linear conductor of length \(l\) as the charge per unit length,
\(\lambda = \dfrac{q}{l}\)
so its unit is the unit of charge divided by the unit of length. Since charge has dimensions \([\text{T}\,\text{I}]\), the dimensions of \(\lambda\) are \([\text{L}^{-1}\text{T}\,\text{I}]\).

For comparison, the surface charge density \(\sigma = q/A\) is measured in C/m\(^{2}\) and the volume charge density \(\rho = q/V\) in C/m\(^{3}\).

The SI unit of electric dipole moment is the coulomb-metre, C m. It is also expressed in the debye (D), where \(1\,\text{D} = 3.33 \times 10^{-30}\) C m (Sec. 10.9).

The dipole moment is defined as
\(\vec{p} = q(2\vec{l}\,)\)
the product of the magnitude \(q\) of either charge and the distance \(2l\) from the negative to the positive charge, so its unit must be the unit of charge multiplied by the unit of length. It is a vector, directed from the negative charge to the positive charge.

As an example from the chapter, two charges \(+e\) and \(-e\) separated by one angstrom give a dipole moment of \(1.6 \times 10^{-29}\) C m, which is 4.8 D.

The relative permittivity of a medium, also called its dielectric constant, is the ratio of the absolute permittivity \(\varepsilon\) of the medium to the permittivity \(\varepsilon_{0}\) of free space (Sec. 10.4.2):
\(K \text{ or } \varepsilon_{r} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_{0}} = \dfrac{F_{\text{vac}}}{F_{\text{med}}}\)

Equivalently, it is the ratio of the force between two point charges placed a certain distance apart in free space to the force between the same two charges placed at the same distance in the given medium. Being the ratio of two quantities of the same kind it is a pure number and has no dimensions. It is also called the specific inductive capacity.

Since \(\varepsilon_{r}\) is greater than 1 for every material medium, a material medium always REDUCES the force between two charges. For water \(\varepsilon_{r} = 80\), so two charges a given distance apart in water repel or attract with only \(1/80\) of the force they would exert at the same separation in vacuum.
